modelImplications: Cultivated edible olives already have a commercial history on parts of Buenos Aires coast. Absence of a literature pin is not absence of cultivation.
Winter tree-survival minima, spring-bud/flower frost, and autumn fruit frost affect different parts of the crop cycle. Annual minima alone cannot predict reliable harvests.
Rainfed mode makes arid irrigated western commercial valleys look less favorable than rainier coasts. Compare identical water assumptions before drawing regional quality conclusions.
Humid Uruguay can match Mediterranean average managed fruit yields while having poor annual regularity. The data do not justify classing all humid climates unsuitable.

Use globally available rainfall seasonality/absence of a dry quarter as an additional disease-management and production-variability screen; retain warm-season wetness and label as proxy. Literature supplies mechanism, not a calibrated rainfall-to-yield probability.

Monthly normals and annual RH cannot represent rain frequency, canopy wetness duration, spring frost timing, pollination, disease control, soil drainage, or alternate-bearing state. Confidence and numeric model scope must disclose these gaps.

CHELSA annual RH at native INIA orchard pixels is~58-60%, whereas local paper discusses Uruguay annualRH70-78% and station bloom-monthRH>70%Oct/>60%Nov. These differ in period/spatial support, so avoid a made-up global RH correction or treating an annualRH70% threshold as a definitive screen.
